extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors and educators designing/assessing writing and presentations for nonmajors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for student-written mathematics papers and oral presentations aimed at non-major audiences; focuses on mathematical correctness, organization, audience-appropriate form and content, and communicative techniques. Intended to help instructors teach and assess communication in mathematics courses for nonmajors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is mathematically correct and complete; reasoning is correct and explicit about assumptions, definitions, and premises when applying theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From notes: identify “thinking process”; understands the modeling process (e.g., makes assumptions; defines consequences); accurate use of terminology/conventions; correct and consistent use of notations and symbology; in word problems, variables (quantities) are defined unambiguously; definitions are precise; the conclusion is clear and unambiguous; reasoning (logical/mathematical/quantitative) is correct; when theorems are applied, shows how all premises are met; shows how definitions apply.
Use in assessment: check that models state assumptions and consequences, that applications of results explicitly verify hypotheses, and that conclusions are unambiguous. Examples/anti-patterns: omitting assumptions, sloppy notation, or applying a theorem without checking hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for effective communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization and presentation of the work should make content easy to follow and find; sentences and surface features must be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From notes: well organized with a start, support, and conclusions; presentation is organized around the logic of the problem; organized ideas flow logically; algorithmic process is shown in a logical and organized way; organized on page; it is easy to find info. Sentences are complete, grammatically correct, and logically sound, and spelling is correct. Objective (when applicable). Tonally consistent: writer has in mind a specific mathematical level when writing. For presentations: presenter articulates and looks at audience; handwriting/slides should be legible.
Assessment guidance: evaluate structure alignment with logical argument, clarity of sectioning and guiding text, grammatical correctness, and presentation delivery (eye contact, articulation, legibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content for effective communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multiple communication modes and well-chosen examples/visuals to make the explanation accessible to the target audience; motivate and explain the problem, not just give the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From notes: multiple communication modes are used–words, graphics, models, etc., so the explanation can reach all members of the target audience. Appropriate use of graphics (diagrams, charts, graphs). Good choice of examples for concepts/definitions; well illustrated (good examples) to promote understanding of concepts. Well motivated to capture interest (why does the reader/listener want to know this?). The problem is explained, not just the answer, so an uninformed reader understands the whole picture. Set up correctly (variables defined; problem introduced). Assumptions are clearly stated. 
Practical notes: each example and visual should be designed to achieve particular objectives (help readers understand a point, concept, or definition). Avoid relying solely on symbolic manipulation without explanatory text or visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form appropriate for audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The form and style of writing/presentation should match the audience's needs—clear, succinct, appropriately detailed, and balanced between words and symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From notes: clear; thorough yet elegant; complete–including all details necessary for audience understanding; succinct; deliberate word choice; appropriate balance of words and symbols: words are used to explain and/or motivate that which is demonstrated with symbols.
Assessment hints: check whether level of detail is neither too elementary nor too compressed, whether symbolic work is accompanied by explanatory prose, and whether wording is chosen deliberately for the audience's level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content appropriate for audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Material should be pitched to the target audience in tone, level of technicality, and engagement; anticipate audience questions and respect audience norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From notes: content is pitched appropriately to the target audience; for example, definitions as appropriate; choice to use technical language or not as appropriate. Addresses the understanding level and questions of the audience. Tone is enthusiastic to keep the reader interested. Interesting/engaging (e.g., choice of examples, choice of presentation style, writing voice). Gives a story of the human experience in the problem, either their own or something out of history. Respectful of the audience (e.g., in group work, constructive group-work skills; for presentations, well prepared). Asks questions which will lead to discussions.
Practical cues: evaluate audience alignment by checking choice of vocabulary, whether necessary background is provided, and whether the presentation anticipates typical confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics not categorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Other desirable personal and rhetorical attributes that contribute to effective communication but do not fit earlier categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From notes: achieves intended or desired goal; something about elegance; demonstrating self-reflection/metacognition; confidence. 
These are higher-level or affective criteria—assess whether the piece achieves its pedagogical or communicative purpose, demonstrates thoughtful reflection on the mathematics or exposition, and displays confident delivery or voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content is mathematically correct and complete.
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph-form statement: reasoning is correct and clearly communicated; assumptions and consequences are identified; when theorems are applied, indicate how premises are met and how definitions apply, leading to a clear conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Expanded guidance from paragraph: Notation, conventions, and terminology are used correctly and consistently. Anything new is defined precisely; for example, in word problems, variables are defined unambiguously. The paper answers the assignment. 
Use this as a checklist for mathematical correctness and completeness when grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing is crafted to convey content effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph-form statement: the paper is carefully organized so the structure of reasoning is clear and information is easy to find; the organization matches the logic of the problem and the structure is communicated to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples from paragraph: organization via guiding text, page formatting, and text formatting. Sentences are complete, grammatically correct, logically sound, and spelling is correct. The paper targets a consistent audience and is appropriately objective. For presentations, audio and visuals are crafted to convey content effectively; the presenter articulates and looks at the audience, and handwriting/slides are legible.
Assessment: judge structure, clarity of guiding text, surface correctness, and presentation mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content is designed to guide audience to understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph-form statement: motivation and context are provided as needed to help the audience understand the big picture and follow reasoning; groundwork and introductions are provided appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From paragraph: begin by eliciting audience interest, build audience understanding, and provide groundwork as needed (e.g., introduce concepts, precise definitions, state assumptions). Use multiple communication modes–words, examples, visuals, models–so explanation reaches the target audience. Each example and visual should be designed to achieve particular objectives (help readers understand an important point, concept, or definition).
Assessment: look for evidence of scaffolding, motivation, and intentional choice of multimodal supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing is carefully crafted for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph-form statement: text should be succinct, deliberate, and elegant while facilitating audience understanding; include necessary details and omit unnecessary wordiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From paragraph: words are used to explain or motivate symbolic work; unnecessary details and wordiness are omitted. Tone, level of detail, and correctness should inspire reader confidence in the author.
Assessment: evaluate conciseness, deliberate diction, and whether choices build author credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content is carefully designed for the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph-form statement: design content to meet audience needs—engaging examples, meta-cognitive commentary, respectful tone, and anticipation of audience questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
From paragraph: craft content to be interesting and engaging (lively tone, interesting examples, thought-provoking questions, human stories). Include helpful meta-cognitive commentary where appropriate to help readers think about the problem or see connections. Treat the audience with respect (collegial tone, careful revision, constructive group participation). Provide definitions only as needed and use technical language only when it aids understanding; anticipate and address audience questions.
Assessment: check engagement strategies, meta-cognitive supports, and audience-respectful tone.
